dossier.architecture: First-year swerve scorer with carefully staged cargo and a reverted climber.

subsystems.drivetrain: First swerve season after differential drive; team emphasized driver practice.
subsystems.intake: Nonparallel four-bar with carbon/foam roller and printed mecanum features; passive deployed flap bridges the bumper gap.
subsystems.transfer: Single-roller ramp; wrong-color cargo rejected using an alternative turret aim.
subsystems.scoring: Aluminum/nitrile main wheel with brass inertia disks; back wheels reduce spin. Wheel idles throughout the match and changes speed with range.
subsystems.endgame: First-regional pivot/telescope replaced by faster four-stage design at regional 2; reliability problems led to a return to original architecture for Worlds with wider hooks and a second rear hook. Reported 15–20 seconds.
subsystems.controls: LED shooter-readiness feedback supports driver decisions.

versions: Three distinct climber states: original, faster replacement, revised original at Worlds.
dossier.analysis: A reverted design is a real season evolution, not missing progress. Count successful retained climbs and total match contribution rather than treating a faster prototype as a superior final robot.
limits: Only the reviewed published configurations are established; intermediate changes may be undocumented.

context_documents.title: 2022-5172 · A fast rejected climb is not the same as a useful fielded climb
context_documents.body:
# 2022-5172: A fast rejected climb is not the same as a useful fielded climb

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A nonparallel four-bar and passive bumper-gap flap feed a ramp and turreted launcher with added brass inertia. The team says a faster two-arm climb had mechanical problems, so it reverted and widened hooks to clear the turret/reduce swing.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The source explicitly prioritizes the revised reliable climb over the failed fast alternative.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

Useful timing includes completion probability and physical interference. A turret that scores well can still block the climb’s swept envelope. Continuous wheel idling also has an electrical/thermal cost that should be measured.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test hook clearance over turret range, climb swing and repeated-volley wheel recovery.

## Limits

Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

## Sources and navigation

- [https://youtu.be/5pX6RHlKFR0](https://youtu.be/5pX6RHlKFR0)

source_reviews.title: Behind the Bumpers 5172 Gators Robot | Rapid React
source_reviews.locator: 1:33–2:57 drive, 3:05–4:26 intake, 4:34–6:45 conveyor and turret, 6:53–8:11 climb
source_reviews.review_basis: Read the timestamped English transcript in the public player panel. Mechanism account is from interviewed team members at Championship.
facts: First-year swerve separated translation and rotation on the driver’s sticks. The pneumatic nonparallel intake dropped a Lexan bridge and used a foam roller with carbon core and printed mecanum elements.
One conveyor wheel set staged cargo. A sensor near the top classified color, and the turret diverted the wrong color. The flywheel stayed running with RPM set from Limelight range.
The team reverted its second regional’s four-stage climb, widened the hooks for turret clearance and replaced a single hook with two to reduce swing.
limitations: Automatic transcription supports sequence and rationale. Exact hardware dimensions, solenoid plumbing, angle limits and reliability sample were outside the review. The 15–20 second climb is team-reported at Worlds.

source_review.whole_robot_explanation: The Gators combined a compliant over-bumper collector and a short mechanically simple ramp with an independently aimed launcher. The launcher also served as the reject exit. The Worlds climber was a revised return to an earlier rung-transfer architecture, with the turret’s physical width directly shaping the hook layout.
source_review.piece_flow: Floor cargo encounters the foam roller, whose larger angled end contacts guide it inward. On deployment a Lexan guard drops to give cargo a surface over the bumper and into the chute. A single set of conveyor wheels moves the ball up the ramp and holds it before release. The color sensor near the top decides whether to shoot toward the hub or rotate the turret to discharge away from it. The flywheel supplies launch speed and the upper compliant contacts reduce backspin. Exact locations and sequence for two simultaneously held cargo were not explained.
source_review.packaging_and_motion: Swerve can translate while the turret changes azimuth, although the collector still has an approach side. The lift has a powered hook for reaching and lifting, then a deployable support-hook geometry for changing the suspended chassis angle. At Worlds the hooks had to clear the turret across that transition. The useful clearance check follows the suspended chassis and full turret sweep through the complete sequence, including sway and asymmetric engagement.

subsystems.name: Drive and operator feedback
subsystems.construction: Swerve chassis with separate translation and rotation inputs. LEDs visible to driver and operator.
subsystems.operation: Driver translates independently of heading. Dark blue denotes lined up and ready, while lighter blue denotes close to alignment.
subsystems.team_rationale: Driver emphasized the practice needed to learn the new drivetrain and valued maneuverability.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: A shared ready indication can keep the driver moving until the shot is usable. It needs to distinguish stale vision from a genuinely good alignment.
subsystems.interfaces: Chassis heading sets intake presentation and remaining turret travel. Vision and readiness states reach both operators.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Recheck gyro orientation and sensor/LED agreement after impacts or restarts.
subsystems.unknowns: Swerve module model, heading reset and exact ready predicates.

subsystems.name: Pickup and bridge
subsystems.construction: Pneumatic nonparallel four-bar, foam roller around a carbon-fiber rod, printed angled contacts and a deployable Lexan guard.
subsystems.operation: The guard drops as the intake deploys and bridges into the chute. Larger end contacts funnel off-center cargo.
subsystems.team_rationale: The team highlighted the bridge as important to bumper crossing and valued compliance for fast pickup against a wall.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: A moving bridge removes a floor-level handoff discontinuity without another powered axis. Its loaded edge still needs overlap with the chute through linkage play.
subsystems.interfaces: First roller to bumper bridge to chute entrance.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Look for a curled guard lip, a binding hinge or damaged end prints when pickup succeeds but handoff fails.
subsystems.unknowns: Linkage stops, roller surface speed and guard retention when stowed.

subsystems.name: Staging and rejection
subsystems.construction: Ramp, single conveyor wheel set and color sensor near the top.
subsystems.operation: The wheels hold cargo until feed. An opposing color triggers a different turret azimuth and discharge.
subsystems.team_rationale: The alternate heading keeps the rejected cargo from scoring in the hub.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Sharing the shot path saves a second exit but can interrupt the next scoring cycle during slew, discharge and reacquisition. A color decision must stay associated with the correct cargo.
subsystems.interfaces: Sensor decision to indexing release and turret aim.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Test alternating colors and closely spaced cargo, with particular attention to whether a second piece advances during reject.
subsystems.unknowns: Reject angle, sensor timing and simultaneous two-ball inventory.

subsystems.name: Turret launcher
subsystems.construction: Limelight, aluminum main wheel with blue nitrile tread and brass inertia masses, plus compliant upper wheels.
subsystems.operation: Automatically aims turret. Changes the speed of an already-spinning flywheel with observed range.
subsystems.team_rationale: Brass supports speed retention, nitrile improves grip and reducing backspin was intended to reduce bounce-outs.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Added inertia reduces instantaneous RPM loss at release and makes large speed changes slower at a given torque. Keeping the wheel running reduces cold spin-up delay.
subsystems.interfaces: Conveyor exit, range-to-speed map, azimuth and readiness feedback.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Check tread and upper contact wear before recalibrating. Verify collision envelope at all useful azimuths.
subsystems.unknowns: Hood mechanism, exit-spin measurements and electrical duty cycle.

subsystems.name: Worlds climber
subsystems.construction: Powered reach hook and deployable support hooks. Wider hook placement and paired support contact distinguish the return configuration.
subsystems.operation: Reach mid, pull into support hooks, deploy to set reach angle, then reach the next bar and repeat.
subsystems.team_rationale: The four-stage replacement had mechanical issues. Wider hooks cleared the turret and paired contact reduced swing.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Once the rung is supporting the chassis, changing hook geometry also moves the whole chassis and changes the next reach target.
subsystems.interfaces: Rung contact, suspended chassis pitch and turret envelope.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Test a one-sided catch and a missed latch under load. Look for unequal contacts and interference before the next reach.
subsystems.unknowns: Exact actuator/rigging details and cause of the four-stage faults.

revisions: First regional used the earlier hook architecture. The second used the faster four-stage unit. Worlds returned to the earlier architecture with clearance and anti-swing changes.
transferable_principles: Evaluate climb upgrades by completed hangs per attempt and deadline margin. Test transitions with the scoring package installed.
disconfirming_conditions: A shared rejection exit loses its appeal if mixed-color traffic repeatedly holds up good cargo. Wider hooks only improve integration if they clear the turret and partners across the loaded sweep.
remaining_gaps: Event-specific reliability, electrical load and a section through the two-ball path remain open.

recommended_images.purpose: Seek source stills for the deployed bridge and Worlds hook clearances. Timestamp targets are from the transcript.
